## Summary

**Background.** Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is increasingly
used to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), but may increase
infection risk compared with established prophylaxis. We evaluated
survival, GVHD, and infection outcomes.

**Methods.** We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS to April 30, 2026,
for studies comparing PTCy-based prophylaxis with alternatives in adults
undergoing allo-HSCT. Comparisons were PTCy versus calcineurin inhibitor
(CNI) plus methotrexate or mycophenolate (C1), versus anti-thymocyte
globulin (ATG; C2), and between PTCy-based regimens (C3). Outcomes
included overall survival (primary), non-relapse mortality, acute GVHD,
CMV reactivation, bloodstream infection (BSI), and invasive fungal
infection. Odds ratios (ORs) were pooled by Bayesian random-effects
meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261372156).

**Findings.** Of 4145 records, 250 studies (523 arms; 177 849 patients)
were included, 105 in the meta-analysis. Versus CNI-based prophylaxis,
PTCy was associated with lower odds of death (OR 0·73, 95% credible
interval 0·58–0·89) and of grade II–IV acute GVHD (0·58, 0·44–0·76). CMV
reactivation was more frequent but uncertain (1·20, 0·87–1·65), and more
so in studies published from 2020 (1·43, 0·97–2·06); the BSI estimate
was larger but based on four studies (2·17, 0·86–4·39). Versus ATG,
survival favoured PTCy imprecisely (0·75, 0·43–1·28) and CMV
reactivation did not differ (0·86, 0·51–1·42). Certainty of evidence was
very low for all prespecified outcomes.

**Interpretation.** PTCy was associated with less GVHD and possibly
better survival than CNI-based prophylaxis, with possible but
imprecisely estimated increases in CMV and bacterial infection. The CMV
pattern fits an effect of T-cell depletion depth, whereas a similar BK
virus increase against both comparators suggests a
cyclophosphamide-specific effect. These associations support close viral
monitoring rather than avoidance of PTCy.

**Funding.** There was no funding source for this study.

## Research in context

::: panel
### Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS from database inception to April
30, 2026, for systematic reviews and meta-analyses of post-transplant
cyclophosphamide (PTCy) in allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell
transplantation, using the terms "post-transplant cyclophosphamide" AND
("meta-analysis" OR "systematic review"). We found ten comparative
meta-analyses,[@yu2019; @poonsombudlert2019; @gagelmann2019;
@arcuri2019; @gao2021; @arcuri2021; @tang2023; @luo2025; @jin2025;
@shahsavand2026] each including 6–30 studies. All examined survival and
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), but only three[@tang2023; @luo2025;
@jin2025] pooled infection outcomes, with few studies per infection and
comparator. None compared PTCy with both calcineurin inhibitor
(CNI)-based and anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)-based prophylaxis, so it
remained unclear whether infections seen with PTCy reflect the drug
itself or T-cell depletion in general.

### Added value of this study

This systematic review (250 studies; 177 849 patients) is the first to
evaluate survival, GVHD, CMV, bloodstream infection, and invasive fungal
infection together, comparing PTCy with both a less T-cell-depleting
regimen (CNI plus methotrexate or mycophenolate) and a more depleting
one (ATG). CMV reactivation was more frequent with PTCy than with
CNI-based prophylaxis (odds ratio 1·20, 95% credible interval 0·87–1·65)
but not compared with ATG (0·86, 0·51–1·42), a pattern compatible with
the comparators' depth of T-cell depletion, although a formal test did
not confirm the difference (ratio of odds ratios 0·71, 0·41–1·20). BK
virus reactivation, by contrast, was increased to a similar extent
against both comparators.

### Implications of all the available evidence

PTCy is associated with less GVHD and better overall survival than
CNI-based prophylaxis, although certainty of evidence is very low and
adjustment for publication bias weakened these benefits. Infection risks
differ by pathogen: CMV risk may follow the depth of T-cell depletion,
whereas BK virus risk may be specific to cyclophosphamide. For
clinicians, this argues for close CMV and BK virus monitoring and for
strategies that support immune recovery (optimised letermovir
prophylaxis, earlier tapering of immunosuppression, adoptive T-cell
therapy) rather than avoiding PTCy. Different PTCy-based regimens showed
no detectable differences, but with three to six studies per outcome
this is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence.
:::

## Introduction

Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) is
potentially curative for many haematological malignancies, but
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a major cause of morbidity and
mortality after transplantation.[@zeiser2017] GVHD prophylaxis must
therefore strike a difficult balance: enough control of donor T cells to
prevent GVHD, without unduly delaying immune reconstitution, weakening
the graft-versus-leukaemia effect, or increasing susceptibility to
infection.

Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has substantially changed this
balance. Developed for haploidentical transplantation, it enables
transplantation across HLA barriers and has made haploidentical donors a
widely available alternative when no matched donor
exists.[@odonnell2002; @luznik2008] Its use has since extended to
matched related and unrelated donors,[@kanakry2016] and in the BMT CTN
1703/1801 randomised controlled trial (RCT), PTCy-based prophylaxis was
superior to conventional calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-based prophylaxis
for GVHD-free, relapse-free survival.[@bolanosmeade2023]

These benefits must be weighed against effects on immune recovery.
Cyclophosphamide given on days +3 and +4 preferentially eliminates the
proliferating alloreactive T cells responsible for GVHD,[@kanakry2013;
@wachsmuth2019] but may also slow recovery of pathogen-specific
immunity,[@zhao2022] which matters because infections remain major causes of non-relapse mortality after allo-HSCT.[@styczynski2020]

Whether PTCy itself increases infection risk is uncertain. Compared with
CNI-based prophylaxis, CIBMTR registry studies have reported more
cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation[@goldsmith2021] and bacterial
bloodstream infection (BSI) with PTCy, with similar or fewer invasive
fungal infections (IFI).[@papanicolaou2024] These signals are
biologically plausible, but infection risk after transplantation also
depends on donor type, conditioning intensity, graft source, GVHD and
its corticosteroid treatment, and antimicrobial prophylaxis, so
associations with PTCy need not reflect a direct effect of
cyclophosphamide.

The key clinical question is therefore whether the infection profile of
PTCy is specific to the drug or a consequence of intensive T-cell
depletion in general. If the latter, similar infections would be
expected with other strongly T-cell-depleting regimens; if particular
infections are more frequent with PTCy than with both less and more
depleting approaches, a cyclophosphamide-specific effect becomes more
likely. Comparing PTCy against both a less depleting comparator (CNI
plus methotrexate or mycophenolate) and a more depleting one
(anti-thymocyte globulin \[ATG\]) offers a way to separate these
explanations. No previous meta-analysis compared PTCy with both; each included 6–30 studies and focused mainly on GVHD and survival rather than infection.

We therefore did a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of
PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis in adults undergoing allo-HSCT, evaluating
survival, non-relapse mortality, GVHD, and infection outcomes across
three prespecified comparisons: PTCy versus CNI plus methotrexate or
mycophenolate, PTCy versus ATG, and different PTCy-based regimens.

## Methods

### Search strategy and selection criteria

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance
with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO
(CRD420261372156). We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from database
inception to April 30, 2026 for studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD
prophylaxis with alternative regimens in adult (≥18 years) allo-HSCT
recipients published in English. The complete search strategy for PubMed
is provided in the [appendix (pp
2–4)](appendix-preview.html#s1.-search-strategy). Reference lists of
included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched. No language
restrictions were applied at the search stage; studies not available in
English were excluded at full-text review.

Studies were eligible if they reported at least one pre-specified
outcome with extractable event counts (numerator and denominator) for at
least two arms differing in GVHD prophylaxis strategy. Conference
abstracts were excluded. We defined three pre-specified comparisons: C1,
PTCy (with or without CNI or mycophenolate mofetil \[MMF\]) versus CNI
plus methotrexate (MTX) or MMF without ATG or T-cell depletion; C2, PTCy
versus ATG-based prophylaxis; and C3, within-PTCy regimen variants.

Two reviewers (MS and REL) screened titles and abstracts using the
Covidence platform (www.coevidence.org) and extracted data from PDFs
files into a structured template ([appendix p
5](appendix-preview.html#s3.-characteristics-of-included-studies)) using
AI tools (Claude Code, Anthropic, Inc.). All extracted values were
manually verified by two investigators against source publications. Risk
of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I for observational studies and RoB 2
for RCTs. Studies sharing patient cohorts were flagged and the most
comprehensive publication was designated as primary publication for each
cohort–outcome combination. All pooled estimates reported here were
derived from this cohort-deduplicated dataset, so that no patient
contributes more than once to any single outcome. The cohort overlap map
is provided in the [appendix (p
24)](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap).

### Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), analysed as all-cause
mortality (death as the event) at the reported timepoint. Secondary
outcomes included non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV
(at day +100), chronic GVHD (moderate to severe), CMV reactivation
(any), bloodstream infection (BSI, any pathogen), invasive fungal
infection (IFI, any), relapse-related mortality (RRM), BK virus
reactivation, and infection-related mortality (IRM).

### Statistical analysis

We fitted Bayesian random-effects binomial-logistic regression models
using `brms` (version 2.23.0) with an `rstan` backend in R (version
4.6.0). The primary model (M1) estimated the PTCy treatment effect with
a random intercept and a random PTCy-effect slope for study, so that
pooled effects average over between-study heterogeneity in the treatment
effect. Each study contributed a single row per outcome with a preferred
timepoint where reported (day +100 or +180 for early outcomes, one year
for late outcomes), otherwise the nearest reported (fallback) timepoint
was used so no within-study correlation across timepoints arises. An
indicator variable distinguished fallback from preferred timepoints.
Weakly informative priors were specified: N(0, 2·5) on fixed effects,
N(0, 1·5) on the intercept, and Student t(3, 0, 1) on the between-study
standard deviations (τ). Four chains of 4000 iterations (1000 warmup)
were run with `adapt_delta` = 0·95 (increased to 0·99 where divergent
transitions occurred). Convergence was assessed by R̂ and effective
sample size. Single-arm descriptive studies (n = 26) were retained for
the PRISMA flow diagram and descriptive tabulation only; because they
report no comparator arm, they contribute no outcome data to any
comparative model, all of which are restricted to studies reporting
event counts for both a PTCy and a non-PTCy arm. Arms receiving PTCy
together with anti-thymocyte globulin were classified as PTCy arms in
all three comparisons; a sensitivity analysis excluding the C2 studies
containing such arms is reported in appendix S9.

An exploratory steroid-adjustment model (M2), a post-hoc amendment to
the registered protocol (appendix S13), added arm-level systemic
corticosteroid exposure as a covariate. Because the covariate is
post-treatment and arm-level, and in most arms approximated from acute
GVHD incidence rather than directly reported, M2 estimates no indirect
effect and is reported only in the appendix (S9), together with its
definition, provenance, results, and a matched-set comparison against
M1.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses included restriction to publications
from 2020 onward (a publication-year, not enrollment-era, subset,
spanning the letermovir-introduction period), to haploidentical-dominant
cohorts (≥50% haploidentical donors), and leave-one-out analysis. Hazard
ratios were not pooled in the primary analysis because most studies
reported only event counts or Kaplan–Meier estimates at fixed
timepoints; in a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, the reported
overall-survival hazard ratios (multivariable-adjusted where available,
one per study, direction harmonised to PTCy versus comparator with death
as the event) were pooled two-stage under a random-effects model
(appendix S9). Frequentist random-effects models (restricted maximum
likelihood \[REML\], `metafor` version 5.0.1) were fitted as concordance
checks. Publication bias was assessed using robust Bayesian
model-averaging (RoBMA). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the
GRADE framework adapted for observational evidence.

### Role of the funding source

There was no funding source for this study.

## Results

### Search results and study characteristics

The search identified 4145 records (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS
481), of which 1220 were duplicates (@fig-prisma). After screening 2925
titles and abstracts, 517 articles were sought for full-text review; 52
could not be retrieved or were not in English. Of 465 full-text articles
assessed, 215 were excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n215)),
leaving 250 studies for the systematic review. Of these, 105 contributed
outcome data to the meta-analysis: 72 compared PTCy with CNI plus
methotrexate (MTX) or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) (C1), 27 compared PTCy
with ATG (C2), and 13 compared different PTCy-based regimens (C3); seven
studies contributed to more than one comparison (per-outcome attrition
in appendix S12).

The 224 comparative studies included 518 treatment arms and 177 461
patients (@tbl-characteristics). Most were retrospective cohorts (131
\[58%\]) or registry studies (62 \[28%\]); only 14 (6%) were RCTs.
Median publication year was 2023 (IQR 2021–24) and median follow-up 26
months (22–36).

PTCy was used mostly in haploidentical transplantation (126 \[46%\] of
PTCy arms), whereas comparator arms were mostly matched unrelated (94
\[38%\]) or matched sibling (54 \[22%\]) donor transplants. Because
donor type itself influences GVHD, infection, and survival, this
imbalance was addressed in sensitivity analyses.

### Risk of bias

Of 210 comparative observational studies assessed with ROBINS-I, 142 (68%) were at serious and 68 (32%) at moderate risk of bias, mainly because of
confounding by donor type and conditioning intensity; none was at low or
critical risk ([appendix pp
15–17](appendix-preview.html#s5.-risk-of-bias)). Of the 14 RCTs
(assessed with RoB 2), 11 had some concerns, two were at high risk, and
one was at low risk. Measurement concerns (three trials) affected clinician-judged outcomes such as GVHD grading and infection ascertainment, not objective outcomes such as mortality or laboratory-confirmed BSI.

### PTCy versus CNI plus MTX or MMF

#### Survival and GVHD

Compared with CNI plus MTX or MMF, PTCy was associated with better
overall survival (k = 29; odds ratio \[OR\] 0·73, 95% credible interval
\[CrI\] 0·58–0·89; @fig-os). Non-relapse mortality (NRM) showed a trend
towards benefit, but the estimate was uncertain (k = 11; 0·84,
0·48–1·28), and relapse-related mortality was modestly lower (k = 34;
0·87, 0·76–0·99). The effect on GVHD was more consistent: PTCy was
associated with less grade II–IV acute GVHD (k = 28; 0·58, 0·44–0·76)
and less moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD (k = 18; 0·41, 0·23–0·72).

#### Infections

The infection findings were less consistent than the GVHD findings. CMV
reactivation was more frequent with PTCy on average, but the credible
interval included no difference (k = 21; 1·20, 0·87–1·65; @fig-cmv). The
estimate was larger in studies published from 2020 onward (k = 16; 1·43,
0·97–2·06) and in haploidentical-dominant cohorts (k = 12; 1·34,
0·89–1·96). In the primary BSI analysis, restricted to culture-confirmed
infection by day +100, the odds were about twice as high with PTCy (k =
4; 2·17, 0·86–4·39), but with only four studies this estimate is highly
uncertain; no BSI model was possible for comparison 2. BK virus
reactivation showed the clearest signal, and was the only infection
outcome whose credible interval excluded no difference (k = 11; 2·39,
1·41–3·73; @fig-infections). There was no clear difference in IFI (k =
6; 0·63, 0·19–2·44), an estimate based on few studies with extreme
between-study variation (τ = 1·28). Infection-related mortality was not
increased with PTCy (k = 13; 1·02, 0·67–1·50).

### PTCy versus ATG

Fewer studies compared PTCy with ATG, so these estimates were less
certain. Overall survival favoured PTCy, but not conclusively (k = 6;
0·75, 0·43–1·28), as did acute GVHD (k = 7; 0·53, 0·23–1·17) and
relapse-related mortality (k = 10; 0·79, 0·55–1·03). NRM could not be
assessed because only two studies provided usable data. The infection
pattern differed from comparison 1: CMV reactivation did not differ
between PTCy and ATG (k = 12; 0·86, 0·51–1·42), nor did
infection-related mortality (k = 7; 0·98, 0·62–1·77). BK virus
reactivation was again higher with PTCy (k = 3; 2·49, 1·08–6·24),
although this estimate rests on only three studies.

### Different PTCy-based regimens

We found no clear differences between PTCy-based regimen variants for
overall survival (OR 1·05), NRM (0·55), acute GVHD (0·31), chronic GVHD
(0·60), or relapse-related mortality (0·78); all credible intervals
included no difference. With only three to six studies per outcome, this
reflects insufficient evidence to detect a difference, not evidence that
the regimens are equivalent.

### Sensitivity analyses

The main findings were broadly unchanged in sensitivity analyses
(appendix S9). Within individual studies, the proportion of
haploidentical donors differed little between arms (median difference
0), adjusting for this difference did not change any comparison 1
estimate, and restricting to studies with closely matched donor types
(difference ≤15 percentage points) strengthened rather than weakened the
survival association (k = 21; 0·58, 0·41–0·78). Trial-only analyses were
not possible, because no more than two trials per outcome reported
observed event counts; analyses restricted to observational studies gave
results similar to the main analysis (overall survival 0·79, 0·63–0·96,
k = 26; acute GVHD 0·59, 0·44–0·78, k = 27; chronic GVHD 0·48,
0·27–0·86, k = 14; NRM 0·91, 0·57–1·36, k = 10; CMV 1·01, 0·64–1·64, k =
7). Pooled overall-survival hazard ratios (mostly multivariable-adjusted) showed a consistent but attenuated effect (hazard ratio 0·88, 0·66–1·14, k = 14; count-based
OR in the same studies 0·75, 0·57–0·93).

The survival association appeared stronger against CNI plus MTX (0·56,
0·34–0·84; k = 12) than against CNI plus MMF (1·10, 0·44–3·01; k = 5),
but a formal test did not confirm that the comparator backbone explains
this difference (ratio of ORs 1·82, 0·76–4·53). For CMV, restricting to
clinically significant infection rather than any reactivation gave an
estimate compatible with both a decrease and an increase (0·94,
0·49–1·71; k = 8), which does not establish that clinically significant
CMV infection is unaffected by PTCy. Adjusting for a letermovir
enrolment-era proxy did not change the CMV estimate (1·20, 0·86–1·67).
No arm in the 2020-onward subset had recorded letermovir use, and most
of these cohorts enrolled before or across the letermovir era, so the
larger recent estimate cannot be attributed to letermovir.

### Certainty of evidence

Certainty of evidence (GRADE) was very low for all prespecified outcomes
(@tbl-results; [appendix
S10–S11](appendix-preview.html#s11.-grade-certainty-of-evidence-profiles)),
mainly because of the predominance of observational studies, risk of
confounding, between-study inconsistency, and imprecision. Imprecision
was judged against clinically meaningful thresholds (OR 0·80 for
benefit, 1·25 for harm). Every prespecified outcome was downgraded for
imprecision except C1 acute GVHD, whose interval lay entirely below
0·80; this outcome was nevertheless rated very low because of
inconsistency and publication bias. Among secondary outcomes added by
protocol amendment, certainty was low for BK virus reactivation versus
CNI-based prophylaxis and very low for the remainder (appendix S11).

Publication-bias analyses (robust Bayesian model-averaging) found strong
evidence of bias for both overall survival and acute GVHD in comparison
1 (Bayes factors for bias 10·4 and 10·9). After adjustment, both
estimates were close to no effect (overall survival 0·97, 0·71–1·16;
acute GVHD 0·96, 0·57–1·38; appendix S10), so the size of the unadjusted
benefits should be interpreted cautiously.

## Discussion

This systematic review and meta-analysis of 250 studies (over 177 000
patients) evaluated the benefits and infection risks of PTCy-based GVHD
prophylaxis within a single analytic framework. Its central finding is
that the infection profile of PTCy may depend on both the comparator and
the pathogen.

### Survival and GVHD

The reduction in GVHD is consistent with how PTCy works: given shortly
after transplantation, it targets the rapidly dividing donor T cells
responsible for alloreactivity.[@kanakry2013; @wachsmuth2019] In
comparison 1, PTCy was associated with about 108 fewer cases of grade
II–IV acute GVHD per 1000 patients (from a median comparator-arm
incidence of 33%) and about 68 fewer deaths per 1000 patients by one
year (from a median comparator-arm mortality of 35%). Better GVHD
control may reduce the need for prolonged immunosuppression and
corticosteroids, which contribute to both infection and non-relapse
mortality: GVHD and its treatment are leading drivers of non-relapse
mortality,[@zeiser2017] and an exploratory steroid-adjustment analysis
(appendix S9) was compatible with this pathway. These findings extend
the matched-donor result of BMT CTN 1703[@bolanosmeade2023] across donor
types, conditioning regimens, and geographic settings, although the ATG
comparison was underpowered relative to comparison 1.

### CMV

The odds of CMV reactivation were about 20% higher with PTCy than with
CNI-based prophylaxis, with substantial uncertainty, but were not
increased compared with ATG. One explanation is that CMV risk follows
the depth of T-cell depletion rather than cyclophosphamide itself:
CNI-based prophylaxis, PTCy, and ATG deplete T cells to increasing
degrees, and impaired CMV-specific cellular immunity is a key
determinant of reactivation.[@zhao2022] The data cannot prove this. A
formal comparison of the two pooled CMV estimates did not resolve the
difference (ratio of ORs 1·41, 0·76–2·54), nor did a meta-regression on
comparator class pooling both datasets (k = 33; 0·71, 0·41–1·20;
appendix S9). Moreover, the two comparisons enrolled different
populations (mainly haploidentical transplants in comparison 1, matched
donors in comparison 2), so differences between them may reflect the
patients rather than the prophylaxis. The depletion-depth ordering
(CNI-based \< PTCy \< ATG) is therefore a hypothesis compatible with the
data, not a demonstrated hierarchy. One external comparison supports it:
in a meta-analysis of haploidentical transplantation, CMV reactivation
was more frequent with combined ATG–PTCy than with PTCy alone (risk
ratio 1·42, 1·03–1·95) but similar to ATG alone (1·04,
0·74–1·45).[@luo2025]

### BK virus

BK virus showed a different pattern: the increase was almost identical
against CNI-based prophylaxis and ATG (OR 2·39 *vs* 2·49; ratio 0·96,
0·33–2·50). This is compatible with a cyclophosphamide-specific effect
rather than a general effect of T-cell depletion; cyclophosphamide is a
recognised cause of haemorrhagic cystitis, of which BK virus
reactivation is a major driver after allo-HSCT.[@kaphan2021;
@ruggeri2015; @chorao2025] With only three prior-influenced studies versus ATG, this interpretation is preliminary.

### Bacterial and fungal infections

The data suggest a possible increase in bacterial BSI with PTCy, but
with four studies the size of this risk cannot be established. There was
no convincing evidence that PTCy affects IFI: the few available studies
were highly heterogeneous, probably reflecting differences in antifungal
prophylaxis, and the estimate is compatible with anything from a large
reduction to a large increase. Importantly, infection-related mortality
was not increased.

### Balancing benefits and risks

For clinicians, PTCy should not be regarded simply as "higher-risk" or
"lower-risk" for infection. The data instead suggest a trade-off: better
GVHD control and possibly better survival, alongside greater
susceptibility to selected infections, particularly CMV and BK virus.
Absolute effects are more informative than ORs here. At the median
comparator-arm rates, the CMV OR of 1·20 corresponds to about 46
additional reactivations per 1000 patients by day +100 (a relative risk
of about 1·09 at a 48% baseline), and refers to reactivation rather than
clinically significant disease; the BK OR of 2·39 corresponds to about
134 additional cases per 1000 patients from a 13% baseline, although BK
definitions and screening varied between studies. These findings support
careful CMV and BK virus monitoring in patients receiving PTCy,
appropriate antiviral prophylaxis such as letermovir,[@marty2017] and
prompt treatment of clinically significant infection. They do not
justify avoiding PTCy because of infection concerns; mitigation is more
likely to come from strategies that improve immune recovery, such as
effective CMV prophylaxis, earlier tapering of unnecessary
immunosuppression, and adoptive transfer of pathogen-specific T cells;
future studies should measure immune reconstitution alongside infection
outcomes. The larger CMV estimate in recent publications remains
unexplained, but was not attributable to letermovir.

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, most evidence was
observational; although sensitivity analyses were generally consistent,
residual confounding by donor type, conditioning intensity, transplant
platform, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and centre practice cannot be
excluded. Second, infection definitions varied (for example, any CMV
reactivation versus clinically significant infection; any positive blood
culture versus BSI requiring intensive care). Third, several estimates
rest on few studies (four for BSI, six for IFI, three for BK virus
versus ATG), and with two arms per study the random-effects model is
just-identified, so for sparse outcomes (k ≤ 6) the priors materially
influence the estimated between-study variation and credible intervals
should be read as lower bounds on the true uncertainty. Fourth, IFI
showed extreme heterogeneity, probably reflecting antifungal prophylaxis
and local practice. Fifth, cohort deduplication removed the largest
registry publications from seven outcomes where a smaller series reports
the same patients in more detail, so the survival and chronic GVHD
analyses rest on fewer patients than the size of the review suggests
(appendix S12). Finally, publication bias is a concern: the survival and
acute GVHD benefits were substantially attenuated after adjustment, so
the magnitude of benefit in the primary analysis should not be assumed
to be the true treatment effect. Similarly, the absence of differences
between PTCy-based regimens, with three to six studies per outcome, does
not support flexibility in dosing or backbone selection.

In conclusion, PTCy-based prophylaxis was associated with less acute and
chronic GVHD and better overall survival than CNI plus MTX or MMF,
although this evidence was predominantly observational and weakened by
publication-bias adjustment. The infection findings were
pathogen-specific: possible increases in CMV reactivation and bacterial
BSI versus CNI-based prophylaxis, the most consistent increase in BK
virus reactivation, and no clear CMV increase versus ATG. Whether CMV
risk follows T-cell depletion depth and BK risk follows cyclophosphamide
itself remains a hypothesis. The evidence supports a benefit–risk
trade-off: PTCy provides effective GVHD control, and clinicians should
remain attentive to CMV, BK virus, and potentially bacterial infections.
Given the very low certainty of evidence, these findings should inform,
not replace, adequately powered randomised trials.

## Contributors

REL, MS, and DPK developed the study protocol. REL and MS performed the
searches, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and statistical
analysis, and MS wrote the first draft of the report. MS and REL
verified the extracted data. DPK revised the manuscript. All authors had
full access to all the data in the study and had final responsibility
for the decision to submit for publication.

## Data sharing

Individual study-level data extracted for this systematic review,
including the complete extraction database and analytic datasets, are
available on a public GitHub repository
<https://github.com/lewis-id-lab/ptcy-infection.git>. The manuscript
source, including the notebooks that generate every table and figure, is
available with a rendered version for review at
<https://lewis-id-lab.github.io/ptcy-infection/>. The study protocol is
registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261372156).

## Use of artificial intelligence

AI-assisted extraction (Claude Code, Anthropic, Inc.) was used to aid
data extraction from original PDF source documents, and Posit Assistant
(Posit, Inc.) was used as an aid in R statistical code debugging within
the Positron integrated development environment. AI-extracted values
were manually verified against source publications. The authors take
full responsibility for the analysis and manuscript contents.

## Figures

![**Study selection (PRISMA 2020 flow diagram).** 4145 records were
identified from databases (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS 481) and
1220 duplicates removed. 2925 records were screened and 2408 excluded at
title and abstract. 517 reports were sought for retrieval; 52 were not
retrieved or not in English (not recorded as separate counts). 465
full-text reports were assessed and 215 excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n214)).
250 studies were included in the systematic review; one publication
entered twice during extraction was removed during revision (appendix
S12). 105 unique studies contributed outcome data to the meta-analysis
(C1 72 studies; C2 27 studies; C3 13 studies; 7 studies contribute to
more than one comparison). Reference lists, citation tracking, and
PROSPERO registrations were also searched but yielded no separately
recorded reports, so the identification-via-other-methods branch of the
diagram shows zero.](figures/Figure1_PRISMA_flow_diagram){#fig-prisma}

{{< pagebreak >}}

![**Forest plot — overall survival, comparison 1 (PTCy vs CNI +
MTX/MMF).** Study rows are raw per-study odds ratios with Wald 95% CIs,
computed from the extracted event counts; the diamond is the pooled
Bayesian random-effects posterior median with 95% credible interval
(primary model M1). Events and totals of each arm and REML
inverse-variance weights are shown beside each study row; a 0·5
continuity correction was applied to zero cells when computing the Wald
intervals. k = 29 after cohort deduplication, removal of one duplicate
publication, and exclusion of cumulative-incidence-derived event counts
([appendix](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap)).](figures/Figure2_OS_forest_setB){#fig-os}

**Forest plots — CMV reactivation.** Individual study odds ratios for
any CMV reactivation, with the pooled Bayesian posterior median and 95%
credible interval. The pooled odds ratio was 1·20 (95% credible interval
0·87–1·65) against CNI-based prophylaxis and 0·86 (0·50–1·42) against
ATG; both intervals include the null, and the formal comparator-class
comparison is unresolved (appendix S9). Events, totals, and REML
inverse-variance weights are shown beside each study row.

![**Forest plots — bacterial, fungal, and BK viral infection risk
